Everyone thinks the S&P is topping.

We're not in 2000. We're in 1992.

Here's the historical parallel that explains why this expansion is just getting started; and why Bitcoin is along for the biggest ride of its life.

The dot-com boom didn't start in 1995. It started in 1968.

A Texan named Thomas Carter won the right to attach his own modem to AT&T's network. The principle that came out of that case: the edge of the network belongs to the user, not the monopoly. That principle quietly built the legal foundation for everything that came after.

Then 25 years of grinding legal wins:
→ 1980-86: Computer II separates the network from the services running on top of it
→ 1984: AT&T finally broken up into 7 Baby Bells
→ 1986: Computer III forces open architecture

By the time HTTP and HTML were invented at CERN in 1989, the legal infrastructure for the internet was already in place. The world just hadn't noticed.

Then 1993: Mosaic browser launches. Anyone with a modem can reach the web for the first time.

Then the floodgates:
→ 1995: Netscape IPO doubles in a day
→ 1996: Telecom Act unleashes investment
→ 1998: Fed eases mid-cycle, fueling the bubble
→ 1999: Qualcomm rises 2,600% in a single year
→ 2000: Nasdaq P/E hits 200; almost 3x the Japanese bubble peak of 80

The total damage by 2000:
+572% Nasdaq over 5 years
+20 million jobs created
+7% GDP growth in H2 1999
Productivity growth doubled, from 1.4% to 2.5%

But here's the thing nobody talks about: that 5-year mania sat on top of 30 years of buildout. The mania was the visible 5%. The setup was the other 95%.

Now overlay AI:
→ 2012: AlexNet (deep learning works)
→ 2017: Google publishes the Transformer paper
→ 2020: GPT-3
→ 2022: ChatGPT (100M users in 2 months, fastest consumer product in history)
→ 2024: Spot Bitcoin ETFs approved
→ 2025: Stablecoin legislation advancing

Sound like 1990 to you? Same here.

The difference this time: AI skipped the 30-year regulatory war. No Ma Bell to break up. No 12-year FCC battles. Innovation, investment, and policy support all landed at once. What took telecom 30 years takes AI maybe 15.

And Bitcoin gets to ride the entire wave from the inside. Born in 2008. Has never lived through a real industrial expansion. Never seen a real mania.

So when Cathie Wood revises her BTC target to $1.5M by 2032, that's not a moonboy take. That's the dot-com timeline applied to crypto.

We're at the 1992 of the AI buildout. The 5-year run hasn't started.

Bitcoin does about 7 transactions per second.

$KAS just hit 5,700.

That's 800x the throughput on a fair-launched proof-of-work chain, and here's why this number matters more than almost anyone in crypto is talking about.

Bitcoin's whole reason for existing was to be peer-to-peer electronic cash.

The 2008 white paper from Satoshi is explicit. The pitch was a payment system that doesn't need banks. Money that moves directly between people, secured by cryptography instead of trusted third parties.

That requires the network to actually move money at the speed money needs to move.

It doesn't.

7 transactions per second across the entire global network. Confirmation times measured in tens of minutes when the chain is congested. Fees that spike to $20+ during periods of high activity.

Try paying for a coffee with that. Try sending payroll to a thousand employees with that. Try running a global remittance flow on it. You can't. The network physically cannot handle it.

Now look at $KAS.

5,700 TPS. Block times measured in milliseconds. Fees that round to zero.

The chain that can actually do what Bitcoin promised in 2008 wasn't built by Satoshi. It was built by someone who looked at Bitcoin's structural limits and decided to fix them, while keeping the things that made Bitcoin valuable in the first place: proof of work, fair launch, no premine, no insiders.

Why does throughput matter so much?

Because no asset can be money if you can't move it fast enough.

Gold isn't money in the modern sense. It's a settlement layer. People don't pay for groceries in gold; they pay in dollars, and the dollars settle (slowly, occasionally) against gold reserves at the institutional level.

Bitcoin is currently in the same category. It's a slow settlement layer pretending to be money. The actual transactions of daily commerce can't run on it.

5,700 TPS opens doors that Bitcoin physically cannot:

Real merchant adoption. Not "we accept Bitcoin" with a 30-minute confirmation wait, but actual payment terminals processing transactions at the speed of a credit card swipe.

Micropayments. The small-dollar transactions that get crushed by gas fees on slower chains. Tipping, content access, machine-to-machine commerce.

Global remittance flows. Workers sending money home across borders without losing 10% to Western Union or waiting three days for a wire to clear.

On-chain commerce at consumer scale. Not the niche Web3 marketplaces you have to seek out, but mainstream e-commerce running on a chain that doesn't break under load.

These aren't theoretical use cases. They're waiting for a chain that can actually handle them.

The bull case for $KAS isn't "it might replace Bitcoin."

The bull case is: Bitcoin can't do its own job. $KAS can.

When the global payment layer actually needs replacing (and it will, sooner than most people think), the question stops being "which crypto." It becomes "which one actually works at scale."

Right now, on the throughput numbers alone, there's only one answer.

October 2025 wasn't the cycle top.

It was a midcycle top so weak it didn't even reach average power law.

The 2013 and 2019 midcycle tops both blew past it. The actual cycle top is still ahead.

Most of crypto Twitter is mourning a top that didn't actually happen. Let me walk you through why.

First, let's get the definitions straight.

A midcycle top is the local high that prints partway through a cycle, not the cycle top itself. Every prior cycle has had one, and they're a normal part of how Bitcoin moves.

Look at 2013. $BTC ran from around $13 in January to about $259 in early April. It peaked, sold off ~85% to roughly $50 by July, then ran all the way to $1,150 by year-end. That April peak wasn't the cycle top. It was the midcycle top. The actual top came eight months later.

The 2019 setup is the same shape, just scaled up.

$BTC ran from ~$3,200 in December 2018 to about $13,800 in June 2019. Then it sold off into the COVID wick at ~$3,800 in March 2020. The actual cycle top didn't print until November 2021 at roughly $69,000. June 2019 was the midcycle top. The cycle top came nearly two and a half years later.

What both of those midcycle tops have in common: they blew well past average power law.

Average power law isn't a magic indicator. It's the regression line drawn through the middle of $BTC's lifetime price action. It's the long-term trend the price oscillates around.

Past midcycle tops cleared average power law convincingly. That overshoot is part of how you tell a real local high from sideways noise. When price punches through the trend line and prints above it, it's signaling enough demand to break the regression.

October 2025 didn't do that.

The "top" everyone is now grieving peaked below average power law. By any prior pattern, that's not a cycle top. That's a local high inside a sideways structure.

Want a number? If October had even matched the 2019 midcycle overshoot, $BTC would have printed somewhere north of $200k. We're nowhere close to that, which is itself the tell.

The four-year cycle zombies are extrapolating from a midcycle high that didn't even break trend. It would be like calling June 2019 the top of the 2017-2021 cycle. Nobody serious did that then. Nobody serious should be doing it now.

The actual cycle top is still ahead. When it prints, it'll be well above average power law, like every previous one. That's not a guess; that's the pattern every cycle has followed for over a decade.

It never existed.

What people called "the cycle" was three macro variables happening to line up. And the people still acting like it's real just cost $BTC roughly $15k of price.

Here's the actual story, plus why the dip you just lived through was self-inflicted by people clinging to a theory the data doesn't support anymore.

For about a decade, three things lined up almost perfectly with the Bitcoin halving calendar:

1. The business cycle. PMI expanded, then contracted.
2. Money printing. QE turned on, then off.
3. Interest rates. The Fed cut, then hiked.

Every "crypto cycle" since 2014 rode the same wave. People credited the halving as the cause. The halving was incidental.

The proof is in the bears. Every prior crypto bear (2014, 2018, 2022) maps cleanly onto PMI rolling over, QE ending, and rates rising. Not "Bitcoin halved 18 months ago, time for a bear." The macro environment did the work; the halving narrative just borrowed credit for it.

Underneath, the Fed lifted rates from 1.25% to 2.5% and ran QT at the same time. The 2022 bear got blamed on Luna and FTX. Underneath, the fastest hiking cycle in 40 years was happening.

Three different surface stories. One identical macro setup underneath. That's the actual playbook.

This time the three variables didn't line up.

PMI is expanding. QE is running. Rates are coming down, not up.

The conditions that created every previous "crypto winter" simply aren't present. The macro side of the cycle isn't there.

posts.topic: The 90/10 wealth transfer (the dumpers paid the holders)
posts.body_style: structural framing, Oct/Nov dip as exhibit, $95k counterfactual, identity-bait close
posts.body:
In every bear market, 90% of holders transfer wealth to 10% of holders.

The dumpers create the discount. The accumulators take it.

The Oct/Nov dip is the cleanest example we've ever seen. Here's what 90/10 actually looked like, and which side you were on whether you noticed or not.

First, the framing. Bear markets are not random price events. They are wealth transfers. The same way a bank run isn't a financial event, it's a coordination event where panicked depositors hand their balances to whoever stays calm.

Crypto bear markets follow the same shape. The supply of coins doesn't change. The number of holders doesn't change much either. What changes is the distribution. Who holds what coins, at what cost basis. Every bear, that distribution shifts dramatically toward the holders who don't sell.

90/10 is approximate. Sometimes it's 80/20, sometimes 95/5. The point is the ratio is always lopsided.

Second, what happened in Oct/Nov.

The four-year cycle zombies dumped. Long-term holders distributed (the on-chain data is unambiguous). Retail panicked. Every wave of selling created a discount for whoever was on the other side of the trade.

The four-year cycle is dead. I've made that case in other posts. But the dumpers didn't know that. They saw the calendar, they saw a shutdown-driven dip, they assumed the bear had arrived. They sold into the assumption.

Whoever didn't sell got the discount.

Third, the cost. If the four-year cycle zombies hadn't dumped, $BTC would be at roughly $95k right now instead of $80k.

That ~$15k delta is the most measurable wealth transfer of the cycle so far. Every dollar of price impact from the dumping went directly to the cost basis of whoever held through it. The dumpers paid $15k per Bitcoin to learn that their thesis was wrong. The holders received $15k per Bitcoin for being right.

Fourth, why this is structural. Every bear is a wealth transfer because every bear is fundamentally a coordination failure. People who would have been better off holding sell anyway, because their information environment tells them the asset is going lower.

Whoever is right about the macro stays. Whoever is wrong leaves. The price discounts the leaving until the right side starts buying.

This is not unique to crypto. Real estate in 2008. Tech stocks in 2002. The mechanism is the same.

Fifth, the implication for next time. There will be another dip. There always is. When it comes, the same pattern will play out. The question is which side of the 90/10 you'll be on.

If you held through October and November, you're already on the 10 side. Stay there.

If you sold, what was the actual signal you used? Was it macro? Was it on-chain? Or was it the calendar?

posts.topic: The AI mania is compressed; the Kaspa window is shorter than people think
posts.body:
The dot-com mania didn't start in 1995. It started in 1968.

Twenty-eight years of telecom infrastructure had to be built before the explosion. Most of those years were spent in court, breaking up Bell, dragging cable through monopoly battles, fighting the regulators who didn't understand what was being built.

AI has none of those drags. Which is why the mania is going to compress harder than the dot-com bulls remember, and why Kaspa's window is shorter than most people think.

The history. AT&T's monopoly on long-distance phone service was the gating item for the entire telecommunications buildout from the late 1960s through the early 1990s. Carterfone (1968) cracked the door for third-party devices. The MFJ consent decree (1982) broke up Bell. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 finally deregulated the last mile.

From the 1996 act to the dot-com peak in March 2000 was four years.

Twenty-eight years of infrastructure → four years of mania.

The AI parallel. Foundational compute (transformer architecture, GPU scale, internet-scale data) has been getting built since roughly 2012. ChatGPT's public moment was late 2022. Frontier model deployment, agentic systems, model-as-API for every business — that build-out is happening now.

There are no AT&T-style monopoly battles. No regulator with the legal authority to block GPT-5 from talking to a database. No equivalent of forced-divestiture decrees slowing the deployment.

The 28-year groundwork phase compressed into roughly 10 years. The 4-year mania phase compresses into roughly 2 to 3.

Where are we right now? The most defensible answer is somewhere between 1995 and 1998. Definitely not 1992. Probably not 2000 yet. The Netscape moment was ChatGPT. The infrastructure overbuild is happening in the data center cycle. The mania is getting paid for in equity right now.

The Kaspa angle. This matters for $KAS because the runway for accumulating PoW exposure at fair-launch prices is shorter than the four-year cycle crowd assumes.

If we're in the AI version of 1996 instead of 1992, the time between 'I have time to position' and 'the mania has already moved' is two years, not eight. Kaspa hits 95% mined supply in that window. The hard-fork milestone lands in that window. The institutional onboarding for PoW-as-a-financial-asset happens in that window.

The mistake people make in compressed timelines is they wait for the same setup they would have had in a slower one. The setup doesn't repeat at the same pace. You either pre-position or you're the FOMO buyer.

First, they hold what they shill. Not "I might add some on the dip." They have the receipts on chain, before the call goes out, in size that means something to them. If they wouldn't risk their own rent on it, they shouldn't be telling you to risk yours.

Second, the community accumulates before the public announcement. My community caught Lab at 8 cents. I didn't say a word about it publicly until we were already up 40x or 50x. By the time the public got the name, we were sitting on most of a 98x. That's the pattern that protects a community. The other pattern, where the influencer announces first and the bag goes to the followers last, is what creates rug season every cycle.

Third, when they're wrong, they say it. Out loud. With a date. Not "we got chopped up a little" or "the trade went against us." A real call gets a real post-mortem.

If your favorite caller doesn't pass those three filters, ask yourself what you're actually paying for. The dopamine of being in a chat that thinks it's about to be rich is not worth the bag.

I'd rather lose a follower for being honest than rug my community for the click. That's the whole job.

posts.topic: The AI expansion thesis, anchored by a FedEx story
posts.body:
The highest concentration of humanity's best ideas is in a cemetery.

Think about that for a second. Every person who ever lived had ideas, plans, prototypes, sketches, businesses they wanted to start, problems they wanted to solve. Almost all of them never built any of it. They didn't have the time, the capital, the team, or the technical skill. They took the ideas to the grave.

For the first time in history, that gap is closing. One person with AI can ship what used to take a team of ten. The Wall Street consensus reads that as a job displacement story. I read it as the largest economic expansion in modern history about to unlock. The smallest companies are about to do what only the biggest used to.

Here's the other side, because it's real and it's coming faster than people think.

I had a FedEx driver deliver my package of frozen meat to the wrong house. He never told me. My neighbor found it overnight, put it in her freezer, and didn't say anything for a week. By the time I got it back, the meat was thawed, refrozen, and the package was destroyed.

A self-driving truck would have logged the GPS coordinates of the actual drop. A delivery robot would have rung the right doorbell. The "AI can't replace humans" crowd keeps moving the goalpost on this stuff. Every job that involves driving a route, carrying a box, or following a checklist is in the firing line, and most of those jobs are not coming back the way they were.

The expansion side and the displacement side are happening at the same time. Whoever positions for both wins. The people who only see one side panic into cash or panic into AI stocks at the top.

For crypto, this is why $TAO and $KAS belong in the same conversation. $TAO is the neutral inference layer for the AI side. $KAS is the neutral money layer for the human side. The more the world races to centralize compute and money, the more valuable the decentralized alternatives become. That's the whole thesis.
